newsitem.title: PANAMA: Panama fires striking air traffic controllers.
newsitem.headline: Panama fires striking air traffic controllers.

text.p: Panamanian authorities on Tuesday started firing air traffic controllers on strike and said they would be replaced with workers from the United States.

"I agree they should be fired if they show up at their posts not to work but just to occupy their seats," President Ernesto Perez Balladares told reporters, as at least 25 of 94 striking air traffic controllers were fired, paralysing Panama's airports.
Panamanian Civil Air Service spokesman Victor de la Hoz said the rest of strikers, demanding better pay and pension benefits, would also be dismissed if they did not show up for work.
He said "air traffic controllers from the United States will be arriving in a few hours to replace the fired workers." He said the replacements worked as air traffic controllers in Panama before.
De la Hoz said traffic at Tocumen International Airport in Panama City, the nation's largest which handles about 200 flights a day, should return to normal by Wednesday morning.
But officials at American Airlines, Continental and KLM said their flights to Tocumen had all been cancelled, most likely until Thursday.

The controllers walked out after talks with the government on a pay hike to $2,000 a month from an average of $600 broke down at the weekend. They also want a package allowing them to retire earlier than the national average of 62 years for men and 57 years for women.
"We tried all weekend to avoid the strike. There are things that are unacceptable. They are paid adequately," Perez Balladares said.

Traffic controller Eladio Santanach disagreed. He said a wage increase has been expected for at least 12 years, since Panama took over air traffic control from the Americans after the signing of the Panama Canal treaty in 1977.
"The Americans made between $8,000 to $10,000 a month. When we took control our base salary was $645," he said. A $5 raise was granted in 1984 and nothing else since.
